title: Polymers
description: Chain-growth and step-growth polymerization, common plastics and fibers, and how structure determines the properties of a polymer.
overview: Plastics, fibers, rubber, adhesives, paints and the biopolymers of living things are all polymers: very long molecules built by joining many small molecules, the monomers. About 400 million tons of synthetic polymers are made each year. A polymer’s properties depend not only on its chemical composition but on how long its chains are, how they are branched or cross-linked, and how they pack together.

This chapter covers the two basic polymerization mechanisms, chain-growth and step-growth, with the main commercial polymers made by each, and then the physical properties that make a polymer a rigid plastic, a flexible film, a fiber or an elastomer.
objectives: Classify polymers by mechanism, composition and architecture.
Write the radical, cationic, anionic and coordination mechanisms for chain-growth polymerization.
Name the monomers and uses of the common addition and condensation polymers.
Use the Carothers equation to relate conversion to degree of polymerization.
Explain tacticity, crystallinity, the glass transition, vulcanization and the difference between thermoplastics and thermosets.

sections.title: Polymers and their classification
body: A **polymer** (from Greek, “many parts”) is a molecule made by linking many **monomers**. The repeating segment is the **repeat unit**, and the number of repeat units is the **degree of polymerization**, n, usually 10³–10⁵, which gives molar masses of 10⁴–10⁶ g mol⁻¹. A polymer of one monomer is a **homopolymer**, and one from two or more monomers is a **copolymer**.

list: By mechanism: **chain-growth** (addition) polymers grow by adding monomers one at a time to a reactive chain end, and no small molecule is lost. **Step-growth** (condensation) polymers form by reaction between functional groups of any two molecules present, often releasing a small molecule such as water.

By thermal behavior: **thermoplastics** soften on heating and can be remolded (polyethylene, PVC, nylon, polystyrene). **Thermosets** are cross-linked during curing, are infusible and decompose rather than melt (epoxy, Bakelite, vulcanized rubber). **Elastomers** are lightly cross-linked polymers that stretch and spring back.

sections.title: Chain-growth polymerization
body: Alkenes polymerize by chain reactions with an initiator that creates a reactive site (radical, cation, anion or metal-bound carbon) on the end of the growing chain. The steps are the usual ones: **initiation**, **propagation** and **termination**.

A radical initiator (benzoyl peroxide, AIBN) decomposes by heat to radicals, which add to the less substituted carbon of the monomer to give the more stable radical. Each propagation step adds another monomer, in microseconds. Termination occurs by combination of two chains or disproportionation, and chain transfer (abstraction of an H from another chain) starts branches. Radical polymerization at high pressure (1000–3000 atm, 200 °C) gives **low-density polyethylene (LDPE)**, highly branched, with a low melting point; the film used for bags. It tolerates water and many functional groups, so it is the most widely used industrial method: polystyrene, PVC, PMMA, Teflon and polyacrylonitrile all form this way.

**Cationic** polymerization (initiated by BF₃/H₂O or strong acids) works with alkenes that give stable carbocations, such as isobutylene (polyisobutylene, in butyl rubber) and vinyl ethers. **Anionic** polymerization (initiated by n-BuLi or amide ions) works with monomers that stabilize a negative charge: styrene, dienes and acrylates. With no termination step, anionic chains stay alive until the monomer is gone, a **living polymerization**. Adding a different monomer then continues the chain as a **block copolymer**, and dispersities are very low. Cyanoacrylate adhesives (superglue) polymerize anionically on traces of moisture.

Ziegler and Natta found (1953–54, Nobel Prize 1963) that TiCl₄ with Al(C₂H₅)₃ polymerizes ethene at low pressure and temperature to **high-density polyethylene (HDPE)**, linear and highly crystalline, and polymerizes propene to stereoregular polypropylene. The monomer inserts into a titanium–carbon bond at a surface site. Soluble **metallocene** catalysts (zirconocene/MAO) give narrower distributions and finer control.

In a vinyl polymer –[CH₂–CHR]ₙ– each substituted carbon is a stereocenter. If all the R groups are on the same side of the chain, the polymer is **isotactic**; alternating, **syndiotactic**; random, **atactic**. Radical polypropylene is atactic and soft and sticky. Ziegler–Natta polypropylene is isotactic, which packs into crystals, giving a strong, high-melting (165 °C) material for fibers and molded parts.

example.title: Radical polymerization of styrene
example.problem: Write the initiation, propagation and termination steps for the AIBN-initiated polymerization of styrene.
solution: Initiation: AIBN decomposes (heat), losing N₂ to give two (CH₃)₂C(CN)• radicals. A radical R• adds to the CH₂ end of styrene, giving the benzylic radical R–CH₂–CH(Ph)•.
Propagation: the benzylic radical adds to another styrene at its CH₂ terminus, again giving a benzylic radical, and repeats about 10³ times.
Termination: two chain radicals combine (head-to-head coupling) or disproportionate (one abstracts an H from the other, giving a saturated and an unsaturated chain end).

check.q: Which polymerization gives living chains and block copolymers?
Why is Ziegler–Natta polypropylene stronger than radical polypropylene?
check.a: It is isotactic and crystallizes; radical PP is atactic

sections.title: Step-growth polymerization
body: In **step-growth polymerization**, two monomers with two functional groups each (A–A and B–B), or one with A and B on the same molecule, react repeatedly. Any two molecules can react, so monomers first form dimers, then oligomers, and only late in the reaction do long chains appear. High molar mass requires near-complete conversion, and a precise 1 : 1 stoichiometry, since an excess of one monomer caps the chains. Wallace Carothers developed the field at DuPont in the 1930s, producing nylon.

Here Xₙ is the average degree of polymerization and p the fractional conversion of functional groups. At 90% conversion Xₙ is only 10; 99% gives 100; and 99.9% gives 1000. Chain-growth polymers, by contrast, have long chains from the start.

example.title: Nylon-6,6
example.problem: Write the equation for nylon-6,6 and its repeat unit.
solution: Each amide link forms with the loss of one water. The name records the number of carbons in the diamine (6) and in the diacid (6). In the laboratory, nylon forms at the interface of an aqueous diamine and an adipoyl chloride solution (the “nylon rope trick”).

example.title: Carothers equation
example.problem: A polyester synthesis reaches 98.5% conversion. What is Xₙ, and what molar mass does it correspond to if the repeat unit mass is 192 g mol⁻¹ (two monomer residues per repeat)?
example.solution: Xₙ = 1/(1 − 0.985) = 67 monomer residues, or about 33 repeat units. The molar mass is about 33 × 192 ≈ 6.4 × 10³ g mol⁻¹, low for a useful plastic, so industrial polyesters are driven above 99.5% conversion by removing the water or glycol under vacuum.

check.q: Why must the monomers be present in a precise 1:1 ratio in step-growth polymerization?
check.a: An excess of one monomer leaves chain ends of the same type and limits chain length

sections.title: Properties of polymers
body: A sample of polymer is a mixture of chains of different lengths, so molar masses are averages. The **number-average** Mₙ = ΣNᵢMᵢ/ΣNᵢ counts each chain equally, and the **weight-average** M_w = ΣNᵢMᵢ²/ΣNᵢMᵢ weights heavier chains more. The **dispersity** Đ = M_w/Mₙ is 1 for identical chains and larger otherwise: about 1.05 for a living anionic polymer, 1.5–2 for radical polymerization, and 2 for step-growth.

example.title: Molar mass averages
example.problem: A sample has equal numbers of chains of M = 10,000 and M = 30,000 g mol⁻¹. Find Mₙ, M_w and Đ.

body: Polymer chains cannot crystallize completely: crystalline regions (**crystallinity** 40–90%) are mixed with amorphous regions. Linear, regular chains pack well (HDPE, 70–90% crystalline, stiff, melting at 130 °C), and branches prevent packing (LDPE, 40–50%, flexible, melting at 110 °C). Amorphous polymers or regions show a **glass transition temperature**, T_g, below which chain segments are frozen and the material is hard and brittle, and above which segments move and the material is soft or rubbery. T_g is about 100 °C for polystyrene and PMMA (hard at room temperature), 80 °C for PVC, and −70 °C for natural rubber (elastic at room temperature). A **plasticizer** (phthalate or citrate esters) lowers T_g, which makes PVC flexible.

**Natural rubber** is cis-1,4-polyisoprene, from latex. Raw rubber is sticky and flows. Heating with sulfur (**vulcanization**, Goodyear, 1839) forms S–S cross-links between chains, so that the polymer stretches and returns to shape. A few percent sulfur makes a flexible tire, and 30% makes hard ebonite. Synthetic rubbers such as styrene–butadiene rubber (SBR), a copolymer, are vulcanized in the same way. Cross-linking converts a thermoplastic into a thermoset and is permanent.

Most polyolefins resist degradation and persist as waste or as **microplastics**. Recycling codes 1–6 mark PET (1), HDPE (2), PVC (3), LDPE (4), PP (5) and PS (6). Thermoplastics can be mechanically recycled by remelting, though the properties degrade with each cycle; thermosets cannot. Bio-based and **biodegradable** polymers are an alternative: **polylactic acid (PLA)**, a polyester of lactic acid made from fermented sugar, degrades by ester hydrolysis in industrial composting. Chemical recycling, which depolymerizes PET with methanol or glycol and recovers the monomers, is under development for mixed waste.

Why is vulcanized rubber elastic and not sticky?
check.a: Sulfur cross-links tie the chains into a network that returns to shape
wrong: Sulfur raises the molar mass only

check.q: Why is HDPE stiffer than LDPE?
check.a: Linear chains pack into crystals; branching in LDPE prevents it
wrong: HDPE has a lower molar mass

quiz.q: A cured epoxy adhesive cannot be melted and reshaped by heating. The reason is that it
quiz.a: is a covalently cross-linked network, so it decomposes before it can flow
wrong: is a linear polymer with a melting point above its decomposition temperature
is a chain-growth polymer, and these never melt
has crystallinity of nearly 100%, so no chain segments can move
quiz.why: Curing joins the chains into one network, which makes the material a thermoset. A thermoplastic has separate chains that slide past each other when heated.

quiz.q: A polystyrene sample has a number-average molar mass of 52,000 g mol⁻¹. The repeat unit, C₈H₈, has a mass of 104 g mol⁻¹. The average degree of polymerization is
quiz.why: The degree of polymerization is the number of repeat units per chain: 52,000/104 = 500.

quiz.q: In the radical polymerization of vinyl chloride, CH₂=CHCl, an initiator radical R• attacks
quiz.a: the CH₂ carbon, leaving the radical on the chlorine-bearing carbon
wrong: the CHCl carbon, leaving the radical on the CH₂ carbon, which is less hindered
the chlorine atom, displacing a chlorine radical from the monomer
either carbon equally, since the double bond is symmetric and the product is the same
quiz.why: Radicals add to the less substituted end of the alkene, so as to give the more stable, more substituted radical. Each propagation step repeats this head-to-tail addition.

quiz.q: What produces the branches in polyethylene made by high-pressure radical polymerization?
quiz.a: Chain transfer: a radical abstracts a hydrogen from a chain and growth restarts there
wrong: Insertion of monomer into a titanium–carbon bond at an irregular site on the catalyst
Termination by disproportionation, which leaves an alkene end that then grows again
Cross-linking of the chains by sulfur atoms that bridge neighboring polymer molecules
quiz.why: Hydrogen abstraction moves the radical to the middle of a chain, and new monomers add there as a side chain. Ziegler–Natta catalysts avoid this and give linear polyethylene.

quiz.q: Which monomer is best suited to cationic polymerization?
quiz.why: Cationic polymerization needs a monomer that gives a stable carbocation, and isobutylene gives a tertiary one. Acrylonitrile and acrylates carry electron-withdrawing groups and suit anionic polymerization.

quiz.q: Styrene is polymerized anionically with n-BuLi until all monomer is consumed. Butadiene is then added to the same flask. What results?
quiz.a: a polystyrene–polybutadiene block copolymer, since the chain ends are still active
wrong: a mixture of polystyrene and polybutadiene homopolymers, with no covalent link between them
a random copolymer of styrene and butadiene, as the two monomers share the active chain ends
no further reaction, because the chains were terminated when the styrene ran out
quiz.why: An anionic polymerization has no termination step, so its chains are living. They add the new monomer and produce a block of the second polymer, with very low dispersity.

quiz.q: TiCl₄ with Al(C₂H₅)₃ polymerizes ethene at low pressure and temperature. The product is
wrong: highly branched low-density polyethylene, formed by chain transfer
polyethylene cross-linked through titanium atoms into a network
a low-molar-mass wax with a branch at each carbon atom
quiz.why: Monomer inserts into the Ti–C bond at a surface site, which avoids chain transfer and gives unbranched chains that pack into crystals.

quiz.q: A sample of polypropylene is a soft, tacky, amorphous solid. It was most likely made by
quiz.a: radical polymerization, which gives atactic chains
wrong: Ziegler–Natta polymerization, which gives isotactic chains
anionic polymerization, which gives living syndiotactic chains
quiz.why: Radical addition does not control the stereochemistry of each CHCH₃ center. The irregular atactic chains cannot crystallize.

quiz.q: One mole each of adipic acid (146 g mol⁻¹) and hexamethylenediamine (116 g mol⁻¹) react completely to give nylon-6,6. Ignoring end groups, what mass of polymer forms?
quiz.why: Each repeat unit contains two amide links, and each link forms with loss of one water. The mass is 146 + 116 − 2 × 18 = 226 g.

quiz.q: What conversion of functional groups does a step-growth polymerization need to reach an average degree of polymerization of 500?
A step-growth polymerization has reached 50% conversion. The average chain contains about
quiz.why: Xₙ = 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2, so the mixture is mostly dimers and small oligomers. Long chains appear only near complete conversion, unlike in chain-growth polymerization.

quiz.q: Which pair of monomers gives Kevlar?
wrong: a diisocyanate and a diol, such as ethylene glycol
quiz.why: Kevlar is an aromatic polyamide. The aliphatic pair gives nylon-6,6, the diacid–glycol pair gives PET, and the isocyanate–diol pair gives polyurethane.

quiz.q: A mixture contains 3 mol of chains with M = 10,000 g mol⁻¹ and 1 mol of chains with M = 50,000 g mol⁻¹. What is the weight-average molar mass M_w?
quiz.why: M_w = ΣNᵢMᵢ²/ΣNᵢMᵢ = (3 × 10⁸ + 1 × 2.5 × 10⁹)/(3 × 10⁴ + 5 × 10⁴) = 2.8 × 10⁹/8 × 10⁴ = 35,000. The number average is 20,000, and the dispersity is 1.75.

quiz.q: Poly(vinyl chloride) is hard at room temperature (T_g about 80 °C). A phthalate plasticizer makes it flexible by
wrong: raising the crystallinity of the polymer
cross-linking the chains into a network
lowering the molar mass of the chains
quiz.why: The plasticizer molecules sit between chains and let segments move at lower temperature. Below T_g the polymer is a hard glass, and above it the segments move and the material is soft.

quiz.q: Rubber is vulcanized with 30% sulfur instead of a few percent. The product is
quiz.a: hard and rigid (ebonite), since heavy cross-linking prevents chain motion
wrong: softer and stickier, since sulfur acts as a plasticizer
more elastic than tire rubber, since there are more cross-links to spring back
a thermoplastic that melts and can be remolded
quiz.why: A few percent sulfur gives a loose network that stretches and recovers. A dense network leaves the chains little freedom, and cross-linking is permanent, so the product is a thermoset.

quiz.q: Polylactic acid can be broken down in industrial composting, whereas polyethylene persists. Why?
quiz.a: PLA has ester links that hydrolyze, but polyethylene has only C–C and C–H bonds
wrong: PLA has a higher glass transition temperature, which makes it chemically reactive
Polyethylene is cross-linked into a network, whereas PLA is a linear polymer
PLA is made by radical polymerization and so contains weak bonds in its chain
quiz.why: Water cleaves the ester bonds in the backbone of PLA, a polyester of lactic acid. The saturated hydrocarbon chain of polyethylene has no such site.

summary: Chain-growth polymers form by adding monomers to a reactive chain end (radical, cationic, anionic, coordination). Step-growth polymers form by reaction between functional groups and need high conversion.
Radical polymerization makes LDPE, PS, PVC and PMMA. Ziegler–Natta catalysts make HDPE and isotactic polypropylene. Anionic living polymerization gives block copolymers.
Nylon-6,6, PET and Kevlar are step-growth polyamides and polyesters. The Carothers equation, Xₙ = 1/(1 − p), shows the need for conversion above 99%.
Mₙ counts chains and M_w weights by mass. Đ = M_w/Mₙ measures breadth.
Crystallinity and T_g control stiffness. Vulcanization cross-links rubber. Thermosets cannot be remolded. Recycling and biodegradable polymers address plastic waste.

problems.q: Draw the repeat units of poly(vinyl chloride), polystyrene and Teflon, and name the monomers.
problems.solution: PVC: –[CH₂–CHCl]ₙ– from vinyl chloride. Polystyrene: –[CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)]ₙ– from styrene. Teflon: –[CF₂–CF₂]ₙ– from tetrafluoroethylene.

problems.q: A mixture of 1 mol of chains of M = 5,000 and 2 mol of chains of M = 20,000 g/mol. Find Mₙ, M_w and the dispersity.
Why can an excess of 2% of diamine in a nylon-6,6 synthesis limit the achievable molar mass, even if conversion is complete?
problems.solution: With a ratio r of the two functional groups, the maximum Xₙ = (1 + r)/(1 − r). Here r = 1/1.02 = 0.980, so Xₙ = 1.980/0.0196 = 101 at most, even at 100% conversion of the limiting group. Both chain ends are then amines and cannot react further.

problems.q: Explain the difference in properties of isotactic and atactic polypropylene.
problems.solution: Isotactic chains have a regular, repeating stereochemistry, so they pack into crystals (melting at 165 °C), giving a strong, rigid solid. Atactic chains are irregular and cannot crystallize, so the polymer is amorphous, soft and tacky.
